content.title: About
content.content: Pecans are the edible seeds of the pecan tree (Carya illinoinensis), native to North America. They have a sweet, buttery flavor and a crunchy texture. Pecans are commonly sold as halves, raw or lightly roasted, and are used in baking, desserts, salads, and as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pecans belong to the hickory family and are closely related to walnuts.
Native American tribes ate pecans and used them in traditional medicine long before European settlement.
The United States is the world’s largest producer of pecans.
Pecans are a key ingredient in the classic Southern dessert pecan pie.
The edible seed is encased in a hard shell; halves are produced by mechanically cracking the shell.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: Pecans provide a high amount of monounsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: They contain vitamin E and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains zinc and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function and normal muscle tone.

items.title: May help regulate blood sugar
items.content: Fiber and healthy fats slow glucose absorption, supporting stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Pecans provide a modest amount of protein useful for vegetarians.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Pecans can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Because they are calorie‑dense, portion sizes should be moderated.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole halves can pose a choking risk for young children.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: People prone to kidney stones may need to limit pecan consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pecans can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, baked goods, and desserts. Raw halves are often used in granola or as a garnish. They can also be lightly toasted with a pinch of salt for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pecans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard any nuts that smell rancid.
